title: Search like a senior
summary: rg, grep, Select-String and editor search: literal versus regex search, the flags people actually use, and a safe search function in C#.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: searching a codebase and its logs
steps.body: Before you change code, find every place it is used; during an incident, find the lines that matter. These are the searches experienced engineers type without thinking.

toolkit.what: ripgrep: recursive, skips .gitignore'd and binary files, and is very fast. The default tool for searching a repository.
flags: fixed string: no regex at all
only files matching a glob (-g '!*.min.js' excludes)
two lines of context around each hit
toolkit.when: finding every caller before you rename or change a method

toolkit.what: Search for text that is full of regex characters without escaping anything.
flags: treat the pattern as plain text
only list the files that match
toolkit.when: searching for IPs, file paths, code like a[0].b or anything with dots and brackets

toolkit.what: grep is on every Linux server and container, even when rg is not. -E switches on extended regex (+, ?, |, {n} without backslashes).
flags: invert: lines that do NOT match
toolkit.when: on a server over SSH, or inside a container with kubectl exec

toolkit.what: PowerShell's grep. It uses .NET regex, and it ignores case unless you add -CaseSensitive.
flags: every match on a line, not just the first
toolkit.when: on Windows machines and build agents

toolkit.what: Search across the whole solution in the editor. The .* button (Alt+R in VS Code) switches the box from plain text to regex; Aa is match case, ab is whole word.
toolkit.example: files to include: src/**/*.cs   files to exclude: **/bin/**, **/obj/**
toolkit.when: when you want to click through the results and edit them in place

steps.prompt: Match each flag to what it does in `rg` and `grep`.
pairs: the pattern is plain text, not a regex
print only the matched part of each line
show lines that do not match

steps.prompt: Complete the command: list the C# files under `src/` that mention the literal text `config.Items[0]`.
steps.explain: `-F` makes the dots and brackets literal, `-l` lists file names instead of every line.

steps.prompt: Which search does each situation call for?
items: Every use of the connection string `Server=db01;Port=5432`
Every ticket key like `OPS-311` in the commit log
Every HTTP status from 500 to 599 in an access log
Lines that start with a date
steps.explain: If you know the exact text, search for it as plain text: nothing needs escaping and nothing surprising can match. Reach for a regex when the text varies.

steps.title: Symptom: the firewall search finds the wrong hosts
prompt: **Symptom.** You search the firewall logs for `10.0.0.1` with a regex tool, and it also returns `10a0b0c1` and `1000001`.
Write the pattern that finds the IP `10.0.0.1` itself. (A neighbour like `10.0.0.12` is a job for the word boundaries
steps.explain: On the command line, `rg -F '10.0.0.1'` avoids the problem entirely.

steps.prompt: `Regex.Escape` makes user text safe to put in a pattern. What does this print?
steps.explain: Every special character gets a backslash. (`Regex.Escape` also escapes spaces and `#`, so the result is safe even in `x` mode.)

steps.title: A tiny grep
prompt: Write `List<string> Grep(string[] lines, string pattern, bool ignoreCase)` that returns the lines in which `pattern`
(a regex) finds a match, in their original order. Pass `RegexOptions.IgnoreCase` when `ignoreCase` is true,
Build the `Regex` **once**, before the loop: constructing a regex parses the pattern, so doing it per line wastes time
starter: List<string> Grep(string[] lines, string pattern, bool ignoreCase)
solution: List<string> Grep(string[] lines, string pattern, bool ignoreCase)
var regex = new Regex(pattern, ignoreCase ? RegexOptions.IgnoreCase : RegexOptions.None);
template: string[] dojoLog = { "09:12 ERROR disk full", "09:13 info ok", "09:14 Error retry", "09:15 WARN slow" };
Dojo.Eq("case-sensitive ERROR", new List<string> { "09:12 ERROR disk full" }, Grep(dojoLog, "ERROR", false));
Dojo.Eq("ignore case finds both errors", new List<string> { "09:12 ERROR disk full", "09:14 Error retry" }, Grep(dojoLog, "error", true));
Dojo.Eq("a class finds WARN and ERROR lines", new List<string> { "09:12 ERROR disk full", "09:15 WARN slow" }, Grep(dojoLog, "[EW][RA]R", false));
Dojo.Eq("no match gives an empty list", new List<string>(), Grep(dojoLog, "FATAL", true));
hints: `var regex = new Regex(pattern, ignoreCase ? RegexOptions.IgnoreCase : RegexOptions.None);`

steps.prompt: Your service searches a 2 GB log for a term a user types. Which line is the safe one?
steps.explain: Escape user input so it is literal, and set a match timeout so no input can keep a thread busy forever. Escaping only dots misses `(`, `*`, `+` and the rest.

steps.title: Search for what the user typed, safely
prompt: Write `int CountMentions(string[] lines, string term)`: how many lines contain `term` as typed, ignoring case.
`term` comes from a user, so it may contain `.`, `(` or `*`.
Build one `Regex` with the escaped term, `RegexOptions.IgnoreCase`, and a match timeout of 250 milliseconds
solution: var regex = new Regex(Regex.Escape(term), RegexOptions.IgnoreCase, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(250));
template: Dojo.Eq("v1.0 in two lines, any case", 2, CountMentions(dojoLines, "/api/v1.0"));
hints: Loop over the lines and count `regex.IsMatch(line)`.
